## Interpreting Results and Formulating Bounded Answers

Numerical results become answers through interpretation. An estimated
difference is an analytical output; a statistical conclusion states
what it indicates about the declared comparison; a substantive
interpretation explains what that comparison means in its setting.
Following this movement keeps the participants, outcome, conditions,
and uncertainty attached to the answer.

### From numerical output to a statistical conclusion

The feedback result is an estimated average assignment effect of
2.50 points, with an approximate 95% interval of 1.00 to 4.00 points
for the eligible cohort. A statistical conclusion can state that
the comparison indicates a positive average effect under the
reported analysis, while retaining uncertainty about its size.
The estimate concerns assignment to a format, rather than the
effect of attending an additional session. It is an average, rather
than a claim that every student benefits by the same amount.

For the dropout rule, the statistical conclusion concerns prediction
on held-out students in the released dataset. The simplified rule
performed somewhat better than the comparison rule using the
dropout proportion from the training data for everyone. This supports a
conclusion about that internal assessment, with performance potentially
varying across other partitions or groups of students. A claim about
future cohorts is a further question, requiring evidence about
prediction in those cohorts and at the intended decision time.

### Substantive meaning, importance, and scope

Units are part of meaning. A difference of 2.50 achievement points
refers to the named delayed assessment and the course topics it
covers. Interpreting it as improved learning depends on what that
assessment measures and when it was administered. A reader should
be able to carry the result back to recognizable tasks students
were expected to perform, rather than treating “achievement” as
an unlimited description of educational benefit.

For an explicitly illustrative comparison, suppose two groups have
recorded dropout proportions of 20% and 30%. Their difference is
ten percentage points. These figures illustrate the unit; they are
not outputs from the fitted student-outcome rule. Whether a support
intervention would reduce dropout remains a separate question.

Bloom and colleagues reported about 13% more calls per week under
home assignment among the 134 order takers included in that analysis
over the nine-month experiment [@bloom2015wfh, pp. 187--188]. This
outcome and subgroup matter: the result concerns weekly calls among
those order takers. “Calls per week” gives the observation period
that turns a count into a rate. Calls per minute of working time
would describe a different aspect of performance.

**Practical importance** connects the size of a result to a
substantive concern. The feedback **protocol**, the document recording
the study's planned decisions before the data were examined, identifies
a two-point improvement as a locally meaningful benchmark. Its
scoring guide awards two points for a fully correct application task,
and the curriculum team judged an average gain of that size worth
considering relative to modest additional preparation. The benchmark
therefore has a stated educational rationale; it is not a universal
threshold for useful feedback.

The estimate exceeds two points, while its interval spans values
below and above that benchmark. The estimated improvement is
positive, with its practical size still uncertain.

In the student case, using probabilities to flag students requires choosing
a cut-off. At 0.5, the rule identifies 73 of the 427 held-out students
recorded as Dropout: $73/427\approx17.0960\%$. Better average probability
predictions can therefore coexist with missing many recorded dropouts at
a selected cut-off. Choosing a cut-off requires considering missed cases
and unnecessary alerts. Recorded dropout is also only one possible sign
of support need. The effectiveness of any subsequent support remains a
separate question; prediction and substantive judgment inform different
parts of that decision.

### Reading numerical results accurately

**Read an estimate with its estimand.** “The difference is 2.50”
gives a number. “The estimated student-average assignment effect
is 2.50 points on the delayed assessment in the eligible cohort”
identifies the quantity it is intended to describe. Keep that
comparison and scope when moving from a table to a written answer.

**Read significance alongside magnitude and uncertainty.** A
small p-value describes incompatibility with a stated null under
stated conditions. A large benefit is a statement about magnitude.
The estimate, its units, and the interval are needed to see how
large and how precisely estimated a difference is; substantive
knowledge helps explain why its size matters.

**Read a nonsignificant finding through its interval and question.**
Using the two-sided test and interval procedure described in Section 4.4,
an illustrative 95% interval from -8 to 8 points contains zero and gives
a nonsignificant result. It leaves
substantial effects in both directions unresolved. An interval from
-0.3 to 0.3 would be much more informative if the study had justified
one point as the smallest important difference. Evidence that an effect
is small needs an appropriate comparison and sufficient precision;
“nonsignificant” alone establishes neither equality nor absence
of an effect.

**Read a fitted model as a specified account of relationships.**
A well-fitting measurement model represents relationships among
the indicators under its conditions. Item content and substantive
knowledge help explain what the factors mean. Similarly, interpreting
a fitted pathway as a causal mechanism needs temporal, measurement,
and design support beyond the existence of a fitted arrow.

**Read results as contributions to an answer.** Retain the outcome,
timing, assessment, and intended use when paraphrasing a reported
conclusion.

### Following the reported answer and its qualifications

Consider these excerpts from the feedback report:

> **Results:** The estimated student-average assignment effect was
> 2.50 points on the 0-40 assessment administered two weeks after the
> six-week program. The approximate 95% confidence interval was
> 1.00 to 4.00 points, with uncertainty reflecting class assignment.
>
> **Discussion:** Assignment to explanatory feedback improved average
> performance on the assessed course topics for eligible students in
> these participating classes, under the reported implementation and
> inferential conditions. Whether the improvement reached the locally
> selected two-point benchmark remained uncertain. Broader learning,
> other settings, and individual effects require additional evidence.

The Results excerpt states the statistical comparison. The Discussion
connects it to course performance while preserving participants,
assessment, conditions, and unresolved magnitude. Reading identifies
what the authors claim. If an exercise asks you to formulate an answer
from supplied results, that answer is your own synthesis. Keeping these
activities recognizable lets a subsequent evaluation examine the
reported claim without silently substituting a different one.

## Connecting Evidence to Answers: The Argument-Based Approach

So far, you have followed a question through its data, design,
analysis, and interpretation. An **argument-based approach** connects
these contributions to the study's answer. An argument here means the
account of how evidence and reasons support an inference and a claim.

One question-answer pair has **one argument with linked layers**. Count
pairs by separately owed substantive answers, rather than by estimates,
tests, or coefficients. Several results can contribute to one answer.
The statistical layer (STAT) concerns recorded variables, statistical
support, analysis, and the statistical conclusion. The substantive layer
(SUB) connects these contributions to the people, practices, meanings,
and setting named by the question. Substantive reasoning enters when a
question and its measures are chosen, as well as when results are
interpreted.

### Recognizing the four functions in Sections 2–5

The four functions already have familiar work to do:

- **Evidence (E):** observations and their production, developed in
  Section 2.
- **Justification (J):** reasons and conditions supporting the comparison,
  developed in Section 3.
- **Inference (I):** analysis and interpretation connecting that support
  to a conclusion, developed in Sections 4 and 5.
- **Bounded claim (C):** the reported answer with its conditions and
  limits, developed in Section 5.

Their logical connection is **E + J → I → C**. Each layer contributes
all four functions, as @tbl-journey-component-definitions explains.
The component names identify what information does in an argument.
A design paragraph, for example, may describe an allocation procedure
and explain why that procedure supports a comparison. These are
different functions within the same paragraph.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
```

| Function | Statistical component | Substantive component | Cross-layer action |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Evidence (E)** | **STAT-E:** information about the observations, variables, and procedures through which the analysis data were produced or acquired | **SUB-E:** information about the people, setting, activities, and substantive meaning represented by those data | SUB-E **situates** STAT-E |
| **Justification (J)** | **STAT-J:** reasons and conditions invoked to support the intended statistical comparison and inference | **SUB-J:** domain-based reasons supporting measurement meaning, implementation, explanation, and applicability | SUB-J **augments and contextualizes** STAT-J |
| **Inference (I)** | **STAT-I:** the analytical reasoning and work connecting evidence and justification to statistical conclusions, including estimates, uncertainty, comparisons, and checks | **SUB-I:** interpretation of that statistical inference in substantive terms, retaining the relevant uncertainty and conditions | SUB-I **interprets** STAT-I |
| **Bounded claim (C)** | **STAT-C:** the reported statistical conclusion about the estimand, with uncertainty, conditions, and scope | **SUB-C:** the reported question-facing answer, with its substantive scope, qualifications, and unresolved matters | SUB-C **bounds** the substantive reach of STAT-C |

: The component functions in the linked statistical and substantive layers. {#tbl-journey-component-definitions tbl-colwidths="[17,30,32,21]"}

The cross-layer arrows in @fig-journey-linked-argument run from the
substantive components to the statistical components they situate,
augment and contextualize, interpret, or bound. These contributions give
statistical work its meaning for the question. They operate alongside
the within-layer support relation, rather than marking separate stages
of research.

```{r}
#| label: fig-journey-linked-argument
#| fig-cap: "One argument with linked layers: logical support and substantive meaning."
#| fig-alt: "Four boxes in the statistical layer are Evidence, Justification, Inference, and bounded Claim. Evidence plus Justification support Inference, which supports Claim. The substantive layer has the same structure. Upward links from the substantive to the statistical components are labeled situates, augments and contextualizes, interprets, and bounds. These links describe logical contributions, not a sequence of research stages."
#| fig-width: 6.25
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-pos: H
par(mar = c(.1, .1, .1, .1), family = "sans")
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 5), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
centres <- c(1.2, 3.65, 6.25, 8.8)
left <- centres - 1.05
right <- centres + 1.05
labels <- c("Evidence", "Justification", "Inference", "Bounded claim")
text(.15, 4.7, "STATISTICAL LAYER", adj = 0, cex = .9,
     font = 2, col = "#315269")
text(.15, .27, "SUBSTANTIVE LAYER", adj = 0, cex = .9,
     font = 2, col = "#267C78")
for (j in 1:4) {
  rect(left[j], 3.55, right[j], 4.3, col = "#E9F0F5", border = "#688AA0")
  rect(left[j], .8, right[j], 1.55, col = "#E9F3F0", border = "#6D9D91")
  text(centres[j], 3.925, paste0("STAT-", c("E", "J", "I", "C")[j],
       "\n", labels[j]), cex = .91)
  text(centres[j], 1.175, paste0("SUB-", c("E", "J", "I", "C")[j],
       "\n", labels[j]), cex = .91)
  arrows(centres[j], 2.85, centres[j], 3.4, length = .07,
         col = "#71818C", lwd = 1.2)
  text(centres[j], 2.5, c("Situates", "Augments and\ncontextualizes",
       "Interprets", "Bounds")[j], cex = .83, col = "#315269")
  arrows(centres[j], 1.72, centres[j], 2.15, length = .07,
         col = "#71818C", lwd = 1.2)
}
for (height in c(3.925, 1.175)) {
  text((right[1] + left[2]) / 2, height, "+", cex = 1.15)
  arrows(right[2] + .06, height, left[3] - .06, height,
         length = .07, col = "#465B66", lwd = 1.3)
  arrows(right[3] + .06, height, left[4] - .06, height,
         length = .07, col = "#465B66", lwd = 1.3)
}
```

Follow the feedback study's Methods, protocol, assessment and
implementation supplement, and analytical supplement through their
extracts in the appendix. @tbl-journey-argument-functions identifies
how these materials contribute to the study's average assignment-effect
argument. Focus on what each contribution does; quality evaluation
considers its adequacy separately.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
```

| Function | Statistical contribution in the feedback study | Substantive contribution in the same argument |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Evidence (E) | **STAT-E:** eligible students and classes; class allocation; assignment, assessment, follow-up, and analysis-sample information | **SUB-E:** who the students are; what explanatory and usual feedback involved; what the achievement assessment represents |
| Justification (J) | **STAT-J:** reasons class randomization, the class-level comparison, declared weighting, and the uncertainty procedure support the assignment-effect inference | **SUB-J:** reasons the assessment meaning, comparable teaching conditions, and delivery records support the educational interpretation |
| Inference (I) | **STAT-I:** the specified analysis; the estimated student-average contrast and its interval; coding, follow-up, and sensitivity checks | **SUB-I:** interpretation of the contrast and uncertainty on the achievement scale at the stated follow-up, against the local benchmark |
| Bounded claim (C) | **STAT-C:** the reported assignment-effect conclusion for the eligible cohort, with uncertainty and inferential conditions | **SUB-C:** the reported answer about assessed performance in these classes and conditions, with its qualifications and unresolved matters |

: Four functions connecting statistical work to a substantive answer. {#tbl-journey-argument-functions tbl-colwidths="[18,41,41]"}

Method families and argument components organize different things.
Regression is a family of statistical tools; its study-specific use
contributes across components. The variables and data contribute
evidence, reasons for the comparison contribute justification, modeling
and estimation contribute inference, and the reported conclusion
contributes a claim. STAT-I usually holds the most technically demanding
statistical work. It traces the central statistical information of the
argument: how evidence, analyzed under the study's stated conditions and
justification, supports a statistical conclusion. Learning methods
develops that reasoning together with an understanding of the evidence
and support it requires.

### Traceable information and where to find it

**Traceable information** is specific study content through which you
can identify an argument component's function at a documentary location.
It may describe an action or state an assumption, interpretation, or
claim. It bridges a general function and the passage or material doing
that work:

**Question-answer pair → argument component → traceable information →
documentary location.**

You can begin with a component and look for its contribution, or begin
with an informative passage and ask what function it performs. For
example, "12 of the 24 classes were randomly allocated to each format" describes
evidence production in STAT-E. The protocol's explanation that this
allocation supports the assignment comparison gives a reason in STAT-J.
The topic is shared, while the particular information performs
different work.

Similarly, "the common assessment was scored without knowledge of
format" describes a measurement procedure in STAT-E. The assessment
blueprint's reasons for treating its tasks as evidence of taught-topic
achievement support SUB-J. Describing which topics the tasks cover
situates the data in SUB-E. Professional knowledge helps you identify
these functions: knowing what random assignment or an assessment
blueprint contributes makes the corresponding information recognizable.
Reading records the offered reasons faithfully; their adequacy is a
further question.

@tbl-journey-study-locations shows where each part of this chain
usually sits in a study's materials.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
```

| Part of the argument | Possible study location | Information a reader may seek |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Question and candidate answer** | Abstract, introduction, or protocol | Purpose, quantitative question, the kind of answer sought (descriptive, associational, predictive, or causal), hypothesis when present, and important planned choices |
| **Evidence and its production** | Methods, data-collection and preparation documentation, instrument documentation, data codebook | Population and unit, recruitment, assignment or exposure, measurement, timing, implementation, exclusions, and completeness |
| **Design and justification** | Protocol, Methods, analysis plan, supplement | Why the evidence, comparison, measurement interpretation, and uncertainty procedure can support the intended move |
| **Analysis and inference** | Results, code, or analytical supplement | Estimates such as differences, slopes, probabilities, loadings, or trajectories; uncertainty; and relevant checks |
| **Bounded answer and reservations** | Discussion and conclusion | Substantive meaning, stated answer, scope, alternatives, and unresolved reservations |

: Where support for a question-answer pair may appear. {#tbl-journey-study-locations tbl-colwidths="[25,31,44]"}

The information's function determines its component. Methods may
contain both production
details and supporting reasons. Results may contain calculations and
claims. A reason may also be distributed across the paper, protocol,
and supplement. Keep a useful page, paragraph, table, or code reference
so another reader can follow your interpretation.

When something consequential remains unclear, describe it in ordinary
language. If a paper and supplement give different follow-up counts,
identify both accounts and the unresolved difference. If you cannot find
how allocation was performed, say which materials you examined and what
their account leaves unclear. This describes the accessible support,
while leaving open what may have occurred beyond the available record.

### Reading first, with quality evaluation available separately

Reading asks what the study's argument contains and how its contributions
fit together. **Quality evaluation** asks whether that support is
adequate for the question and answer. It is a separate, secondary use
that depends on understanding the study. You may notice a concern while
reading and record it alongside your interpretation; identification and
judgment remain distinguishable without requiring two rigid passes.

The six evaluation questions in @tbl-journey-evaluation fall into three
groups: alignment, support, and translation.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
```

| Group | Evaluation question | What to consider |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Alignment** | **Question alignment** | Whether the question, estimand, design, evidence, analysis, and answer remain directed at the same aim |
| **Support** | **Evidence integrity** | Whether the observations and contextual records, their production, and their representation are trustworthy, traceable, and appropriate |
| **Support** | **Justification adequacy** | Whether the statistical, design, measurement, and contextual reasons warrant the proposed moves |
| **Support** | **Inferential adequacy** | Whether reasoning within both layers is adequate, including estimation, uncertainty, checks, sensitivity, and substantive interpretation |
| **Translation** | **Transition fidelity** | Whether the links between layers retain meaning, uncertainty, design status, and scope |
| **Translation** | **Claim calibration** | Whether the reported answer's strength and breadth match its support |

: Six questions for evaluating one question-level argument. {#tbl-journey-evaluation tbl-colwidths="[17,28,55]"}

For an individual evaluation question, use one of four judgments:
**adequate for this purpose**, **needs revision**, **insufficient
information to judge**, or **not applicable**. Add a reason explaining
the particular function or connection being judged.

Consider a variant of the feedback Discussion: "The program produces
important gains in every form of learning for all students." The
numerical results stay the same. Reading identifies the claim;
evaluation identifies why it **needs revision** under Transition
fidelity and Claim calibration. A course-topic assessment has become
every form of learning, and a cohort-average effect has become a benefit
for every student. The claim also settles practical importance more
firmly than the interval permits.

The whole question-answer pair also receives one **whole-pair
conclusion**:

- **Supported as stated:** the available support warrants the answer as
  reported, including a carefully bounded answer that remains
  inconclusive.
- **Supported only after narrowing or revision:** a defensible answer
  remains after correcting its wording, scope, or analytical support.
- **Not supported:** the available record gives sufficient grounds to
  conclude that the proposed answer is unwarranted.
- **Not assessable from the accessible record:** essential information
  for judging the whole answer remains unavailable or unresolved.

The first two conclusions identify an answer warranted by the record,
either as reported or after revision. The last two distinguish an
unwarranted answer from one whose support cannot be assessed from the
accessible record. An argument can fail to support a causal answer
without showing that the effect is absent, and an appropriately
inconclusive answer can still be supported as stated.

The overextended feedback variant is **supported only after narrowing
or revision**, provided the remaining support warrants the narrower
answer. A revised answer keeps the positive average estimate, its
interval, the eligible cohort, the assessed topics and conditions, and
uncertainty about the two-point benchmark. This preserves the original
question while correcting what is claimed for its answer. An unclear
allocation account could instead leave Justification adequacy with
**insufficient information to judge**; a local judgment and a whole-pair
conclusion answer different questions.

A fuller supplementary reading tutorial develops practice in tracing
these contributions, and an advanced supplementary tutorial develops
coordinated questions.

## Conducting Research and Making Its Support Visible

Researchers face the complementary task of producing an informative
study and making its support accessible. Ethics, documentation, and
reporting accompany this work throughout.

### Ethics and responsibility across the study

In the feedback study, participation arrangements, consent where
required,
confidentiality, and fair access to instruction deserve attention before
allocation. Implementation needs to respect those arrangements, and
reporting should describe relevant departures. Protecting students and
preserving an interpretable comparison are connected responsibilities.

In student support, the use of a prediction also matters. A rule with
reasonable average performance may still systematically miss some
students who need help or falsely label others. What follows a prediction
can change the consequences: offering an additional conversation differs
from withholding a service. Understanding those consequences calls for
substantive and ethical judgment as well as statistical evaluation.

In the working-from-home case, linking employee surveys and performance
records also calls for confidentiality and care about employment
consequences. A question about performance can be legitimate while the
handling and use of identifiable records remain consequential.

Responsibilities extend to access and communication. Researchers can
make aggregate results and analysis procedures inspectable while
protecting identifiable student records. An account of exclusions and
missing outcomes lets readers understand whose experience contributes
to the findings. Ethical responsibility belongs throughout the study,
rather than in a final checkbox or a single argument component.

### Reproducibility, reporting, and a visible decision history

A protocol records intended decisions. A data codebook explains the
dataset. An analytical script connects the designated data to outputs.
An assessment guide and implementation account explain their substantive
meaning. Together these materials let a reader follow the support
identified in the location table.

**Computational reproducibility** means that the same data and specified
computations can produce the reported results [@peng2011]. This makes
calculations checkable; design and substantive reasoning determine what
their interpretation supports.

Reporting also preserves the history of decisions. A study can identify
what was planned, what was implemented, what changed, when it changed,
and what evidence was available at the time. Exploratory work has a
legitimate place in that history. Its value is clearer when the reader
can distinguish an analysis suggested by the results from one specified
before those results were examined.

Larger studies require deliberate coordination among analysts, subject
specialists, and authors so that results remain connected to their
questions and support. Interpreting and evaluating that support still
requires their expertise.

### A compact construction-workflow overview

The **construction workflow** organizes the work of developing one
question-level argument in six stages and two phases. It covers much
of the research process, while project administration, collaboration,
and ongoing ethical responsibilities extend across and beyond its
stages. Within this approach, it is an auxiliary use for conducting
research.

**Phase 1: Understand and plan**

1. **Review the problem, setting, and relevant literature.** Develop the
   statistical and substantive reasons for the study.
2. **Frame the question and, where useful, a candidate answer.** State
   what needs answering and its intended scope.
3. **Align design, measurement, estimand, evidence-production or
   acquisition plan, and inferential plan.** Specify how the proposed
   data and analysis will address that question.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
```

**Phase 2: Produce and complete**

4. **Produce or acquire, and document, empirical and contextual
   evidence.** Preserve the observations and the information needed to
   understand their production and meaning.
5. **Estimate, check, and analyse.** Carry out and examine the analytical
   work while recording relevant results and changes.
6. **Contextualize, interpret, and complete the bounded answer.** Connect
   the inference to the substantive question with its uncertainty and
   scope.

Iteration stays within each phase of a cycle: planning can refine the
question and design, while completion can revisit calculations, checks,
and interpretation. The Stage 3-to-4 handoff is one-way within that
cycle. This convention makes prior commitments and their revision
visible; it leaves room for practical research to reuse data and
procedures. For an existing dataset, producing evidence can mean
acquiring or designating the question-specific analysis data.

There are three ways a cycle can end. **Normal completion** preserves
the question, estimand, and prior commitments, even when the answer is
inconclusive or contradicts an expectation. **Phase 2 repair** corrects
work within those commitments, such as a scoring error, and repeats the
affected analysis. Once Phase 2 has begun, changing the question,
estimand, or a prior commitment starts an **additional or revised
cycle**. When the planned evidence cannot answer the original question,
record that cycle as **not answerable as planned**. That label describes
the cycle rather than adding a fourth ending. A new outcome chosen after
examining relevant results receives an explicitly exploratory question and
cycle for those data. A documented revision made before access to those
results can remain prospectively specified; preserve its timing and reasons.
The appendix gives the fuller Phase 1 anchor and
shows how the feedback records keep these commitments visible.

## Reading Bridge

Across the five cases, you can now frame a question and its estimand,
identify the data and how they were produced, and recognize a method
family and the reasons for its use. You can also distinguish an estimate
from its uncertainty and interpretation, then follow the support to a
bounded answer. The argument-based approach connects these contributions
for reading a study. Quality evaluation remains a separate secondary
use, and the construction workflow an auxiliary use for conducting
research.

Chapter 2 builds on this account of how observations arise by examining
recorded data: what the entries
represent, how they are organized, which cases support a calculation,
and how those cases were selected. It then develops distributions, group
summaries, and relationships, applying the design reasoning when
interpreting them.
The same ideas of center, spread, and shape then describe statistics
across repeated samples, giving meaning to sampling distributions and
SE. Statistical inference develops the
calculations and conditions for estimates, intervals, and tests.
Group comparisons bring these ideas together through one-way and two-way
ANOVA, contrasts, and multiple comparisons. Computational practice in R
and regression develop their application further.
Generalized linear models extend the kinds of outcomes a
regression can represent; factor analysis and SEM develop measurement
and linked relationships; mixed-effects models address grouped and
repeated observations.

For further reading, *Introduction to Modern Statistics*
[@cetinkaya2024] connects questions, data, and statistical reasoning,
and *Regression and Other Stories* [@gelman2020] connects regression,
design, and interpretation. Work on estimands [@lundberg2021],
educational measurement standards [@aeraApaNcme2014], and the ASA
statement on p-values [@wasserstein2016] develops specific distinctions.

The argument-based approach is a tutorial synthesis informed by
Toulmin's account of argument [@toulmin2003], LeMire's pedagogical link
between testing and subject-matter claims [@lemire2010], and Kane's
argument-based treatment of interpretation and use [@kane2013]. The
linked components, evaluation questions, and workflow convention bring
those influences together for this tutorial, rather than reproducing
one source's arrangement.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{6\baselineskip}
\phantomsection
```

### Key terms {.unnumbered}

Use this short glossary to revisit the chapter's own vocabulary. The
concept reference in the Part One introduction gives common
alternative names and the main explanation of the statistical ideas
the later chapters develop.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
```

| Term and common alternatives | Meaning |
|:--|:--|
| Question-answer pair | What a study asks and the answer it eventually offers for that question. Each separately owed substantive answer has its own argument. |
| Traceable information | Specific study content through which an argument component's function can be identified at a documentary location. Identifying that contribution precedes judging its adequacy. |
| Estimand | The target quantity sought for the named units, conditions, outcome, and scope. It can concern a fixed dataset, a population, a comparison, or prediction performance. |
| Outcome variable (response variable; dependent variable) | The variable an analysis seeks to describe, compare, or predict. These alternative names share that role in many analyses; a variable's role depends on the question. |
| Predictor variable (explanatory variable; independent variable) | A variable used to represent an outcome's relationship with other information. These analytical-role labels alone establish neither a causal effect nor statistical independence. |
| Sampling (recruitment; selection into a study) | How units come to enter a study, by probability selection, volunteering, or availability. It is contrasted with assignment, which concerns the conditions allocated to participating units. |
| Assignment (allocation) | The allocation of study conditions to participating units, by any mechanism. Actual treatment received may differ from the assigned condition. |
| Random sampling (probability sampling) | Selecting units from a defined population or sampling frame through a probability mechanism that gives every eligible unit a known, nonzero chance of selection, not necessarily the same chance. "Random selection" alone can describe other chance-based decisions. |
| Random assignment (random allocation) | Allocating study conditions to participating units through a specified probability mechanism. The assigned units may be individuals or groups; realized groups need not be identical. |
| Causal effect (counterfactual contrast) | The difference between the outcomes that would occur for the same units or target population under two specified conditions, only one of which is observed for each unit. The contrast may be zero; interpreting a comparison causally needs design and identification support. |
| Confounding | Mixing an exposure's effect with effects of other factors that influence both exposure and outcome. Such a factor is a confounder, a specific causal role. |
| External validity (generalizability) | Support for extending findings to other people, settings, or conditions. The intended extension determines which similarities and differences matter. |
| Unit | The entity selected, assigned, measured, or analyzed in a particular operation. The units of assignment, measurement, and analysis can differ, and all are distinct from measurement units such as points or minutes. |
| Evidence | Observations and contextual records contributing to an answer, including information about how they were produced. |
| Justification | Reasons and conditions invoked to support a comparison, analytical move, or interpretation. |
| Inference | Reasoning and analysis connecting evidence and justification to a conclusion. |
| Bounded claim | The reported conclusion with its uncertainty, conditions, and scope: in the statistical layer, the conclusion about the estimand; in the substantive layer, the question-facing answer with its qualifications. |

: Selected terms for the quantitative research journey. {#tbl-journey-glossary tbl-colwidths="[28,72]"}

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
\phantomsection
```

### Exercise 1: Read a research question and answer (Foundational) {.unnumbered #ex-ch01-01}

Consider this short passage from an invented feedback study:

> We asked whether assigning explanatory feedback rather than the usual
> format would improve delayed achievement for eligible students in
> 24 participating classes. We expected explanatory feedback to help
> students apply the taught material. Classes were randomly allocated to
> the two formats. The estimated average assignment effect was 2.50 points
> on a common assessment two weeks after the six-week program, with a
> 95% confidence interval from 1.00 to 4.00 points. We conclude
> that assignment improved average performance on the assessed topics in
> these classes under the study conditions.

a. Identify the research question, substantive expectation, numerical
   result, and reported answer. Explain how the result contributes to the
   answer and what the answer adds.
b. State the estimand in words, including the comparison, outcome,
   students, and timing. Explain how it differs from the estimate of
   2.50 points.
c. Write a descriptive question that the same assessment records could
   address. Explain how the answer sought differs from the assignment
   effect in the passage.

### Exercise 3: Read design before interpreting a difference (Integrative) {.unnumbered #ex-ch01-03}

Two invented studies concern peer study and course achievement.

- **Study A:** A probability sample of 1,000 students from a university
  reports its weekly participation in peer study. Researchers obtain
  semester grades and compare participants with nonparticipants.
- **Study B:** Among 160 eligible volunteers at the same university,
  researchers randomly assign 80 to an offer of a peer-study program and
  80 to usual study arrangements. All supply semester grades. Some
  students offered the program attend few sessions.

a. Identify how students entered each study and whether the researchers

   What causal question can Study B's assigned-group comparison address,
   and why does it differ from the effect of attending every session?
c. For each study, state a population or group its result could concern
   under the stated design. Identify one piece of further information

### Student outcomes {.unnumbered}

The source follows entrants at the Polytechnic Institute of Portalegre,
Portugal, from 2008/09 to 2018/19. Outcomes were recorded at the normal
duration of their degree: three years, or four for nursing
[@realinho2022]. Recorded Dropout can include a change of course or
institution; Enrolled means still enrolled at that endpoint. Graduate
identifies completion. The released data cover 4,424 students
[@uci697].

The simplified analysis asks how well admission grade and age at
enrollment predict recorded Dropout versus the other two categories
combined. It retains the original categories in the dataset and assigns
about 70% of each binary outcome group to training, leaving the rest
for an internal assessment.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
```

| Dataset | Dropout | Enrolled | Graduate | Total |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Full release | 1,421 | 794 | 2,209 | 4,424 |
| Training | 994 | 562 | 1,540 | 3,096 |
| Held-out test | 427 | 232 | 669 | 1,328 |

: Students in the simplified prediction analysis. {#tbl-journey-student-record tbl-colwidths="[30,17,17,18,18]"}

On the held-out data, average squared prediction error was 0.2000 for
the logistic rule using admission grade and age, against 0.2182 for
predicting the training-data dropout proportion for everyone:

$$
\frac{1}{1328}\sum_i(\widehat p_i-y_i)^2=0.2000\ \text{(logistic rule)}
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad 0.2182\ \text{(training-prevalence rule)},
$$

where $\widehat p_i$ is the predicted probability and $y_i$ the recorded
Dropout indicator, coded 1 for Dropout and 0 otherwise, for each of the
1,328 held-out students.
At a probability threshold of 0.5, the logistic rule
identified 73 of the 427 students with recorded Dropout status, about
17.0960%. Its use for later cohorts and the value of acting on an alert
remain to be established. Semester results
were excluded because they become available after enrollment; the
released file also has no cohort-year field for a later-cohort check.

The data are provided by Realinho, Vieira Martins, Machado, and
Baptista under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/)
[@uci697]. The three fields used here, the binary coding, the split, and
the logistic rule are adaptations for this chapter; the source authors
built other machine-learning classifiers, and the analysis can be
repeated from the public release. Reading the chapter requires no
programming.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{6\baselineskip}
\phantomsection
```

### Feedback {.unnumbered}

The invented report supplies an estimated assignment effect of 2.50
points and a 95% interval from 1.00 to 4.00 points. These quantities support
the chapter's reading exercises; a numerical derivation is outside this
example.

The report and supporting materials describe the study as follows.

> **Paper, Methods:** Twelve participating schools contributed two
> classes each, with 20 eligible students per class. Before the six-week
> program, 12 of the 24 classes were randomly assigned to each format
> across the full class pool. A common 0-40 assessment was administered two weeks after the
> program. All 480 eligible students supplied scores and were analyzed
> according to their class's assignment.
>
> **Protocol, design and analysis:** Random allocation supplies the
> basis for the assignment comparison. Comparing equally weighted class
> means gives students equal weight because class sizes are equal. The
> uncertainty procedure reflects assignment of classes. The inference assumes implementation of the allocation,
> a common outcome definition, complete follow-up, and no influence of
> one class's assignment on another class's outcomes.
>
> **Assessment and implementation supplement:** Both formats used the
> same taught topics and scheduled time. Explanatory feedback added
> explanations of errors; the usual format supplied correctness
> feedback. Delivery logs documented these activities and separate
> materials. The assessment blueprint linked tasks to the topics,
> and scorers worked without knowledge of format. The curriculum team
> judged a two-point gain, equivalent to full credit on an application
> task, worth considering against the additional preparation.
>
> **Analytical supplement:** Checks confirmed the score range, class
> assignments, denominators, and complete outcomes. Recalculating the
> mean contrast with each school omitted in turn left the point estimate
> positive.
> Those reduced-record checks describe influence on the estimate;
> the full eligible cohort remains the basis of the primary answer.

The report concludes that assignment improved average assessed
course-topic performance in these classes and conditions, with the
practical size uncertain and broader learning and individual effects
unresolved. Its Results and Discussion excerpts appear in Section 5.
The separate straight-line and curved plots illustrate relationships
with baseline achievement; their values are separate from the supplied
assignment-effect result.

The **Phase 1 anchor** records the question and mode, estimand, design,
measurement, evidence-production or acquisition plan, inferential plan,
and, where relevant, a stopping rule stating when data collection can
end. Here the protocol commits to the
eligible-cohort assignment effect, formats, delayed assessment, student
weighting, and analysis. The codebook records school, class, assigned
format, pre-program baseline achievement score, delayed assessment score,
and analysis membership. The analysis record connects
those commitments to the contrast, interval, checks, and reported
answer, while dated changes remain visible.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{6\baselineskip}
\phantomsection
```

### Short supporting records {.unnumbered}

**Working from home.** Group counts are 131 assigned to home work and
118 to office work (Appendix Table A.2, p. 214); eligibility and the
nine-month, four-home-day schedule appear on p. 169. Table II, column 4
(p. 187) reports the result for 134 order takers, interpreted on p. 188
as about 13% more weekly calls [@bloom2015wfh]. Other outcomes use
different measures or employee groups. The
[author's paper, appendix, and replication materials](https://nbloom.people.stanford.edu/research)
also include nonexperimental employees for Table IV; record analysis
membership when reusing these files.

**Confidence and belonging.** Confidence concerns handling learning
tasks; belonging concerns acceptance and inclusion in the academic
community. Three 0-100 confidence indicators concern explaining,
applying, and checking; three belonging indicators concern acceptance,
inclusion, and participation. @fig-journey-measurement-map shows a
candidate representation. Each indicator also has variation beyond
its factor; item content, scoring, and occasion help establish what the
representation means.

```{r}
#| label: fig-journey-measurement-map
#| fig-cap: "A candidate measurement map for confidence and belonging. Arrows show proposed measurement relationships; the two-headed link represents a possible factor correlation. Indicator-specific variation is omitted from this sketch."
#| fig-alt: "A confidence factor points to explaining, applying, and checking indicators. A belonging factor points to acceptance, inclusion, and participation indicators. A two-headed link connects the factors. This is a proposed measurement map, not an estimated model."
#| fig-width: 6.25
#| fig-height: 1.25
#| fig-pos: H
par(mar = c(.15, .1, .15, .1), family = "sans")
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(0, 6.5), ylim = c(0, 2.2), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
angle <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = 150)
for (k in 1:2) {
  centre <- c(1.55, 4.95)[k]
  polygon(centre + .72 * cos(angle), 1.7 + .32 * sin(angle),
          col = c("#E9F0F5", "#E9F3F0")[k], border = "#71818C")
  text(centre, 1.7, c("Confidence", "Belonging")[k], cex = .88)
  xs <- centre + c(-1.0, 0, 1.0)
  words <- list(c("Explaining", "Applying", "Checking"),
                c("Acceptance", "Inclusion", "Participation"))[[k]]
  for (j in 1:3) {
    arrows(centre + c(-.35, 0, .35)[j], 1.4, xs[j], .78,
           length = .065, col = "#71818C")
    rect(xs[j] - .48, .25, xs[j] + .48, .7,
         col = "#F7F8F8", border = "#71818C")
    text(xs[j], .475, words[j], cex = .80)
  }
}
arrows(2.35, 1.7, 4.15, 1.7, code = 3, length = .075, col = "#71818C")
```

**Language-learning progress.** The four equally spaced assessments
use a common 0-100 scale. Student A scores 58, 65, 68, and 76; Student B
scores 62, 63, 67, and 68. Their successive gains are 7, 3, and 8 points
and 1, 4, and 1 point, respectively. Student, classroom, school, and
occasion identifiers preserve the grouping and timing. These trajectories
show different starting levels, overall gains, and uneven changes
between assessments. A full growth study would also document other
students, scoring comparability, missed occasions, and changing learning
conditions.
